I'm thinking through where to apply the turn boost in the closed-loop system. In the test sketch it was applied at the duty level for turn-in-place, but with PID velocity control in production, the boost should increase the angular velocity setpoint instead. The PID will naturally compensate for tire scrub through its feedback loop, though there's a wind-up delay involved. The real benefit of turn boost is handling the extra torque needed for turn-in-place due to scrub, and the kickstart behavior matters for responsiveness.

The tricky part is that applying turn boost to the setpoint itself would make the robot turn faster than commanded, which breaks odometry-based navigation since Nav2 expects the actual motion to match the cmd_vel it sends. With closed-loop control, that would mean tracking an incorrect setpoint. So the better approach is to apply turn boost only as an open-loop feed-forward kick, not to the actual setpoint itself.

For the motor inversion logic, I need to be careful about where it's applied. If a motor is wired backward, inverting only the output duty after the PID is the right fix—that way positive duty makes the wheel go forward and the encoder counts positive, preventing the runaway condition where the PID keeps increasing duty trying to match a negative measurement. So I'll define turn_boost as a duty headroom multiplier that applies to the kickstart floor during in-place turns — this captures the physics of increased breakaway torque from wheel scrub. When the robot is turning without linear motion, the kick floor scales up by turn_boost, clamped to max PWM. I'll document this clearly in the tuning parameters. For the kickstart logic itself, I'm detecting when wheels transition from idle to moving and opening the kick window at that moment, then applying the scaled duty floor during the active kick period.

def test_tuning_registry() -> None:
    import tuning

    print("\n[tuning registry]")
    check("all §10 parameters present", len(tuning.PARAMS) == 14,
          f"got {len(tuning.PARAMS)}")

    spec_defaults = {
        "max_pwm_duty": 200,
        "max_linear_speed_mm_s": 300,
        "max_angular_speed_mdeg_s": 60000,
        "lidar_min_range_mm": 150,
        "lidar_max_range_mm": 6000,
        "lidar_angle_filter": [],
        "obstacle_inflation_radius_mm": 150,
        "collision_stop_distance_mm": 100,
    }
    for name, expected in spec_defaults.items():
        check(f"default {name} == {expected}",
              tuning.DEFAULTS[name] == expected,
              f"got {tuning.DEFAULTS.get(name)}")

    accepted, errors = tuning.coerce_updates({"max_pwm_duty": 999})
    check("over-range clamps to 255", accepted["max_pwm_duty"] == 255,
          str(accepted))
    accepted, errors = tuning.coerce_updates({"max_pwm_duty": -5})
    check("under-range clamps to 0", accepted["max_pwm_duty"] == 0, str(accepted))

content.text: The count assertion is a brittle proxy — it was checking "14 params exist" rather than "the §10 params exist". Let me make it check what it actually means, and cover the new block.

check("all §10 parameters present", len(tuning.PARAMS) == 14,
          f"got {len(tuning.PARAMS)}")
input.new_string:
# Assert the §10 table is present by name rather than by count: a count
    # check fails every time an extra parameter is added, which says nothing
    # about whether the spec's parameters are still there.
    spec_10 = {
        "max_pwm_duty", "max_linear_speed_mm_s", "max_angular_speed_mdeg_s",
        "collision_stop_distance_mm", "lidar_min_range_mm",
        "lidar_max_range_mm", "lidar_angle_filter",
        "obstacle_inflation_radius_mm", "encoder_cpr", "wheel_diameter_mm",
        "wheel_base_mm", "pid_kp", "pid_ki", "pid_kd",
    }
    missing = sorted(spec_10 - set(tuning.BY_NAME))
    check("all §10 parameters present", not missing, f"missing {missing}")

    # Motion calibration — the values found on the bench with movement_test.
    # These must be runtime-tunable, not firmware #defines, or retuning the
    # robot means a reflash.
    calib = {
        "invert_left", "invert_right", "trim_left", "trim_right",
        "turn_boost", "kick_duty", "kick_ms",
    }
    missing_calib = sorted(calib - set(tuning.BY_NAME))
    check("motion calibration parameters present", not missing_calib,
          f"missing {missing_calib}")
    check("calibration targets the Arduino only",
          all(tuning.BY_NAME[n].targets == ("arduino",) for n in calib
              if n in tuning.BY_NAME))
    # Trim must never scale *up*: the duty cap is the only thing keeping the
    # 6 V motors safe on an 8.4 V pack, and a >1 trim would eat its headroom.
    check("trim cannot exceed 1.0",
          tuning.BY_NAME["trim_left"].coerce(2.0) == 1.0
          and tuning.BY_NAME["trim_right"].coerce(2.0) == 1.0)
